claims.text: The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles depends on nanoparticle size.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles begin surface-diffusion-driven phase separation earlier during heating than larger nanoparticles.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a nearly equiatomic composition.
In situ aberration-corrected STEM heating combined with molecular dynamics simulations can be used to investigate nanoparticle thermal behavior at the atomic scale.
The proposed FeCuCrCoNi study heats nanoparticles from approximately room temperature to 973 K.
A range of nanoparticle sizes should be studied to capture surface-to-volume-ratio effects.
Heating produces surface diffusion that drives phase separation and superficial layer formation in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio than larger nanoparticles.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio increases the rate of atomic diffusion at the nanoparticle surface.
Enhanced atomic diffusion promotes phase separation during heating.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles form and melt an AuCu surface layer at high temperature.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will form a segregated surface layer or undergo phase separation at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles maintain structural integrity to higher temperatures.
Larger nanoparticles exhibit delayed onset of significant atomic diffusion and phase separation because of their lower surface-to-volume ratio.
The prediction is restricted to nearly equiatomic FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles under conditions where thermal activation dominates atomic mobility.
The exact temperature and size thresholds for phase-separation onset are uncertain.
The hypothesis is falsified if phase-separation onset temperature does not differ significantly between small and large nanoparticles or if structural evolution is independent of nanoparticle size.
